Base
BAYSS
adj.
From Late Latin bassus, low, through Old French. Webster 1828: low in place, in value, in station, or in estimation; mean; vile. The adjective is entirely distinct from the noun meaning a foundation, and the Authorized Version uses the adjective of what God chooses and of what Paul’s critics called him.

Biblical Definition

Base in the Authorized Version means low, of no account, despised. Paul makes it the hinge of the argument that governs the whole doctrine of calling: base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are (1 Corinthians 1:28). The stated purpose follows immediately — that no flesh should glory in his presence. God’s election of the low is not sentiment about the poor; it is a deliberate strategy against boasting, of a piece with reducing Gideon’s army to three hundred. Paul then reports the word being thrown at him: I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you (2 Corinthians 10:1). The Corinthians thought his bodily presence weak and his speech contemptible, and he answers by appealing to the meekness of Christ rather than by asserting himself. Malachi shows the other direction — God makes men base for their partiality: therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have not kept my ways, but have been partial in the law (Malachi 2:9). What God exalts and what He abases are both His own doing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines BASE, a. as low in place; of humble birth or station; mean-spirited; of little comparative value, as base metal; and illegitimate, as base-born. The 1828 senses of low station and low character were still distinguishable, as they are in Scripture.

expand to see more

BASE, a. — Low in place; of humble birth, degree or station; mean; vile; worthless.

Of little comparative value; applied to metals, as base coin, and to any inferior sort.

Deep or grave in sound, as a base voice — a spelling since separated as bass.

Illegitimate; born out of wedlock, as base-born.

The noun BASE, a foundation or pedestal, is from Greek basis and is an entirely different word; the two must not be confused in reading 1 Corinthians 1:28.

Key Scripture

1 Corinthians 1:28 — "And base things of the world, and things which are despised, hath God chosen, yea, and things which are not, to bring to nought things that are:"

2 Corinthians 10:1 — "Now I Paul myself beseech you by the meekness and gentleness of Christ, who in presence am base among you, but being absent am bold toward you:"

Malachi 2:9 — "Therefore have I also made you contemptible and base before all the people, according as ye have not kept my ways, but have been partial in the law."

Psalm 8:4 — "What is man, that thou art mindful of him? and the son of man, that thou visitest him?"

Philippians 3:21 — "Who shall change our vile body, that it may be fashioned like unto his glorious body, according to the working whereby he is able even to subdue all things unto himself."

Modern Corruption

1 Corinthians 1:28 is regularly recruited for liberation readings that make the poor the subject of salvation rather than its recipients, and it is equally abused by a respectability religion that quietly builds churches around the influential.

expand to see more

Liberation theology reads God’s choice of the base as a preferential option that makes the poor the hermeneutical key and the agents of their own deliverance. Paul’s stated reason will not carry it. God chose the foolish, the weak, the base, and the things which are not that no flesh should glory in his presence — the purpose is the abolition of boasting, not the elevation of a class. Poverty saves no one; the same chapter says of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption. The verse humbles the rich without flattering the poor, which is exactly what the gospel always does.

The opposite corruption is more common in comfortable churches and rarely says its name. It is the instinct to build a ministry around the impressive convert, the notable athlete, the man of influence — on the reasoning that God can use such a person more widely. Paul says God’s method is the reverse, and He gave the reason. James forbids the practice outright: the man with the gold ring and goodly apparel and the poor man in vile raiment are not to be seated differently, and to do so is to be judges of evil thoughts. A congregation can tell what it believes about 1 Corinthians 1:28 by who it defers to.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek agenes (G36), of no family, base-born, low; tapeinos (G5011), lowly, humble, in 2 Corinthians 10:1; Hebrew shaphal (H8217), low, in Malachi 2:9.

expand to see more

Greek agenes (G36) — without family, of no birth, base; a hapax legomenon at 1 Corinthians 1:28.

Greek tapeinos (G5011) — low, humble, of no account; in presence am base among you (2 Corinthians 10:1).

Greek exoutheneo (G1848) — to despise, to make of no account; things which are despised in the same verse.

Hebrew shaphal (H8217) — low, humble, base; Malachi 2:9, and Isaiah 57:15 of the God who dwells with the humble.

The English adjective is from Late Latin bassus, low; the unrelated noun is from Greek basis, a stepping or foundation.

Usage

"Base things of the world… hath God chosen (1 Corinthians 1:28) — election aimed at the abolition of boasting."

"In presence am base among you (2 Corinthians 10:1) — the Corinthians’ estimate of an apostle."

"Made you contemptible and base before all the people (Malachi 2:9) — God abasing partial priests."
